Can You Get Dental Implants If You Have Misaligned or Impacted Wisdom Teeth Still Present?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many adults in London who are exploring tooth replacement options find themselves asking a question that may feel quite specific but is surprisingly common: does it matter that my wisdom teeth are still there — and what if they're impacted or misaligned? It's a completely reasonable concern. Wisdom teeth, also known as third molars, are often associated with complications, and naturally, patients want to know whether their presence could prevent or complicate dental implant treatment.

Dental implants with impacted wisdom teeth present is a topic that doesn't always receive a straightforward explanation online, which can leave patients feeling uncertain about whether they're a suitable candidate for implant treatment. Understanding the relationship between third molar position and implant planning is important for anyone considering this procedure.

This article aims to explain the key considerations clearly, outline what a dental professional would typically evaluate, and help you feel more informed before booking a consultation. Individual suitability always depends on a thorough clinical assessment.

Featured Snippet Answer

Can you get dental implants if you have impacted or misaligned wisdom teeth?

Dental implants with impacted wisdom teeth present may still be possible, but suitability depends on a thorough clinical assessment. Impacted or misaligned third molars can affect jaw bone health, infection risk, and bite alignment — all of which are factors a dental professional must evaluate before implant treatment is recommended.

What Are Impacted and Misaligned Wisdom Teeth?

Wisdom teeth typically emerge between the ages of 17 and 25, though for many people they never fully erupt. When a wisdom tooth fails to break through the gum surface completely, or grows at an angle that causes it to press against adjacent teeth, it is described as either impacted or misaligned.

An impacted wisdom tooth is one that remains wholly or partially beneath the gum line, often because there is insufficient space in the jaw for it to emerge properly. A misaligned wisdom tooth (sometimes called angulated) grows in a direction other than vertically — it may lean forwards, backwards, or even sideways.

Both situations can create a range of dental concerns, including:

  • Pressure on neighbouring teeth, which may cause gradual shifting
  • Difficulty cleaning the area effectively, increasing the risk of plaque build-up
  • Localised gum inflammation (pericoronitis) around the partially erupted tooth
  • Potential cyst formation in the surrounding bone tissue
  • Bone resorption in the jaw

The presence of impacted or misaligned wisdom teeth doesn't automatically disqualify someone from implant treatment, but these factors are part of a comprehensive clinical picture that your dental team will need to assess thoroughly.

How Wisdom Teeth Relate to Dental Implant Planning

Dental implants are titanium posts surgically placed into the jawbone to act as artificial tooth roots. For the procedure to succeed, there must be sufficient healthy bone available to support the implant, and the surrounding oral environment must be free from active infection or inflammation.

When wisdom teeth are impacted or misaligned, several factors may influence implant planning:

Proximity to the implant site: If the missing tooth being replaced is near the wisdom tooth — such as a lower second molar — an impacted third molar behind it could physically interfere with implant placement or complicate the surgical approach.

Bone quality and volume: Chronic pressure from an impacted tooth can gradually affect the density or volume of surrounding bone, which is a critical factor in implant success.

Infection and inflammation: Active pericoronitis or infection around a wisdom tooth introduces bacteria that can compromise implant integration during healing.

Bite alignment: A misaligned wisdom tooth that has caused neighbouring teeth to shift may alter bite forces, which are an important consideration in implant positioning.

None of these concerns is necessarily insurmountable, but they all require careful evaluation. Learning more about single-tooth implant treatment and the assessment process can help you understand what to expect during a consultation.

The Clinical Science Behind Implant Success and Third Molar Complications

Understanding why wisdom teeth matter in implant planning requires a basic understanding of bone biology and osseointegration — the process by which a dental implant fuses with the jawbone.

For osseointegration to occur successfully, the surrounding bone must be adequately dense and free from infection. Bone is living tissue that responds to pressure and biological activity. When an impacted wisdom tooth creates chronic inflammation or applies continued mechanical pressure, the body's inflammatory response can trigger osteoclast activity — a process in which bone cells break down existing bone tissue. Over time, this can reduce the volume of available bone in the region.

Bacteria associated with pericoronitis (the gum infection that can develop around a partially erupted wisdom tooth) are also known to affect bone healing. If these bacteria are present at the time of implant placement or during the healing phase, they can interfere with the body's ability to integrate the implant properly.

Additionally, the proximity of tooth roots — including those of impacted third molars — to surgical sites must be assessed using dental imaging such as OPG (orthopantomogram) X-rays or cone beam CT (CBCT) scans. These images allow the dental team to plan implant placement with precision, avoiding damage to adjacent roots, nerves, and sinus structures.

If you would like more detail on this stage, our guide on how dentists avoid nerves and sinuses during implant treatment explains the planning principles in plain language.

Does the Wisdom Tooth Need to Be Removed Before Implant Placement?

This is one of the most common questions patients ask, and the honest answer is: it depends. There is no universal rule that impacted or misaligned wisdom teeth must always be extracted before dental implants can be placed.

In some cases, a wisdom tooth that is fully impacted, stable, not causing infection, and situated well away from the implant site may not need to be removed at all. The dental team will assess whether the tooth poses any foreseeable risk to the implant procedure or long-term outcome.

In other cases, removal may be advisable — or even necessary — before implant treatment proceeds. This is particularly likely when:

  • The impacted tooth is adjacent to the planned implant site
  • There is evidence of active infection or pericoronitis
  • The tooth is causing measurable bone loss
  • The tooth's position would prevent correct implant angulation
  • The tooth is likely to continue causing problems in the long term

If extraction is required, it may be carried out as a separate procedure before implant planning continues, or in some circumstances both procedures can be coordinated as part of an overall treatment plan. Your dental team will explain what approach is appropriate for your individual situation.

Oral Health Factors That Affect Implant Candidacy More Broadly

Wisdom tooth status is just one part of the clinical picture. Dental implant candidacy involves a comprehensive evaluation of overall oral and general health. Factors that your dental team will typically assess include:

Gum health: Active periodontal (gum) disease must be addressed before implants are placed. Gum disease affects the bone and soft tissue that support both natural teeth and implants.

Bone volume and density: Sufficient jawbone must be present to house the implant. In cases where bone loss has occurred, bone grafting may be required before or at the time of implant placement.

General health: Certain systemic conditions and medications — including those affecting bone metabolism — can influence healing and implant success. A full medical history is always taken before treatment.

Oral hygiene: Long-term implant health depends on excellent daily oral hygiene and regular professional maintenance. Patients who struggle to manage their existing oral health may need additional support before committing to implants.

Exploring dental implant eligibility questions in our FAQ section can give you a clearer picture of how your overall oral health plays a role in treatment planning.

When You Should Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

If you have impacted or misaligned wisdom teeth and are considering dental implant treatment, professional assessment is the only reliable way to understand your options. There are also specific situations where seeking dental advice sooner rather than later is advisable, even if implants are not yet your primary concern.

You may wish to speak to a dentist if you are experiencing any of the following:

  • Recurring pain, tenderness, or swelling at the back of the mouth
  • Difficulty opening your mouth fully
  • An unpleasant taste or odour from the back of the mouth (which may indicate infection)
  • Visible swelling around the jaw or cheek
  • Sensitivity or aching in teeth adjacent to the wisdom tooth area
  • Jaw stiffness or discomfort when eating

These symptoms do not necessarily confirm a serious problem, but they are worth having evaluated. Early professional assessment can help prevent minor issues from becoming more complex dental or surgical concerns. If bone loss around an impacted tooth progresses unchecked, it can reduce the volume of bone available for future implant placement, which is why people often ask about options for dental implants with severe bone loss.

Prevention and Oral Health Maintenance in the Wisdom Tooth Area

Even if your impacted or misaligned wisdom teeth are not currently causing symptoms, good oral hygiene in that region can help reduce the risk of complications developing. Here are some practical steps that may help:

Clean thoroughly around wisdom teeth: Use a small-headed toothbrush or single-tufted brush to clean behind the last visible molar. This area is easily missed during routine brushing.

Use interdental aids: Interdental brushes, floss, or a water flosser can help remove debris from around partially erupted teeth where standard brushing cannot reach.

Attend regular dental check-ups: Routine examinations allow your dentist to monitor the position and condition of wisdom teeth over time using periodic X-rays. Changes in position or signs of developing problems can be identified early.

Avoid delaying treatment if symptoms arise: If you notice signs of infection or discomfort around a wisdom tooth, seeking dental advice promptly can help prevent the situation from worsening.

Maintain overall gum health: Healthy gums support healthy bone, and both are essential for dental implant success. A consistent oral hygiene routine and regular professional cleaning form the foundation of long-term dental health.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants with impacted wisdom teeth present may still be possible, but suitability must be confirmed through a thorough clinical assessment.
  • The position, condition, and proximity of the wisdom tooth to the planned implant site are all important factors.
  • Impacted wisdom teeth can affect bone quality, infection risk, and adjacent tooth positioning, all of which are relevant to implant planning.
  • Not everyone with an impacted wisdom tooth will need it removed before implant treatment — this depends on the individual clinical situation.
  • Active infection or gum inflammation must be addressed before any implant procedure is undertaken.
  • Regular dental check-ups and good oral hygiene around wisdom teeth are beneficial for long-term oral health and implant suitability.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can wisdom teeth affect where a dental implant is placed?

Yes, the position of wisdom teeth — particularly those that are impacted or misaligned — can directly influence the placement angle, depth, and positioning of a dental implant. If the wisdom tooth root overlaps with the planned implant site, or if there is insufficient space due to the third molar's location, the surgical approach may need to be modified. Advanced dental imaging, such as CBCT scans, helps clinicians plan around existing tooth structures with precision.

Will I need my impacted wisdom teeth removed before getting dental implants?

Not necessarily. The decision to remove an impacted wisdom tooth before implant treatment depends on several factors, including the tooth's proximity to the implant site, whether it is causing infection or bone loss, and its likely impact on long-term implant health. Your dental team will evaluate your specific case and explain whether extraction is recommended as part of your overall treatment plan.

Can an impacted wisdom tooth cause bone loss that affects implant success?

Over time, chronic inflammation, infection, and mechanical pressure associated with impacted wisdom teeth can contribute to localised bone loss in the surrounding jaw area. Since adequate bone volume and density are essential for dental implant success and osseointegration, this bone loss can affect both candidacy and long-term outcomes. A dental professional can assess the extent of any bone changes using dental X-rays or 3D imaging before recommending a course of action.

How long after wisdom tooth removal can dental implants be placed?

If wisdom tooth extraction is required before implant placement, a period of healing is typically needed before the implant procedure can begin. The length of this healing period varies depending on the complexity of the extraction, the individual's healing response, and whether any bone grafting is required. Your dental team will advise on the recommended timeline for your specific circumstances, which may range from a few months to longer in more complex cases.

Are there signs that an impacted wisdom tooth might be affecting my other teeth?

Possible signs include pain or pressure in the back of the mouth, sensitivity in adjacent teeth, visible swelling of the gum behind the last molar, difficulty cleaning effectively in that area, or shifting of neighbouring teeth over time. However, many people with impacted wisdom teeth experience no obvious symptoms. Regular dental X-rays during routine check-ups are the most reliable way to monitor whether an impacted tooth is causing changes to surrounding structures.

Is there anything I can do at home to manage symptoms from an impacted wisdom tooth while I wait for a consultation?

Maintaining gentle but thorough oral hygiene around the area — using a soft-bristled toothbrush and appropriate interdental aids — may help reduce bacterial build-up. Over-the-counter pain relief suitable for dental discomfort can help manage mild symptoms temporarily, following the packaging instructions. However, home measures are not a substitute for professional assessment. If symptoms are significant, persistent, or worsening, contacting a dental practice to arrange an appointment is the most appropriate course of action.

Conclusion

The relationship between impacted or misaligned wisdom teeth and dental implant treatment is nuanced, and understandably so — it involves multiple clinical factors that interact differently in each patient. What is clear is that dental implants with impacted wisdom teeth present are not automatically ruled out, but a careful, individualised assessment is essential before any treatment decisions are made.

Understanding your oral health situation in full — including the position and condition of any retained wisdom teeth — puts both you and your dental team in the best position to plan a safe and appropriate course of treatment. If you have been considering dental implants and have questions about how your wisdom teeth might factor into your suitability, speaking with an experienced implant dentist is the most reliable next step.
